summary.scoring: genuine catch = the wrong query gets a medium/high finding that the correct query does not get

cases.q: What are the top 5 music genres by revenue, where revenue = InvoiceLine.UnitPrice × InvoiceLine.Quantity summed over all invoice lines of tracks in that genre? Return genre name and revenue rounded to 2 decimals.
cases.mistake: Sums the invoice-level Total once per invoice line, so each invoice's full total is counted repeatedly (join fan-out) instead of summing line amounts.
wrong_detail: After the joins, each `Invoice` row appears 5.44 times on average (2,240 joined rows for 412 Invoice rows). SUM(i.total) therefore adds up the same `Invoice` rows several times.

cases.q: For each customer country (Customer.Country), how many distinct customers have at least one invoice? Show the top 5 countries by that number (ties broken by country name).
cases.mistake: Counts invoices (one row per invoice after the join) instead of distinct customers.
wrong_detail: `customers` is COUNT(*), which counts Invoice rows (412) after the joins - not Customer rows (59).

cases.q: How many tracks were NOT composed by Steve Harris? A track counts if its Composer field does not contain 'Steve Harris'; tracks with no composer recorded (NULL) also count as not composed by him.
cases.mistake: NOT LIKE on a NULL Composer evaluates to NULL, so all tracks with no composer are silently dropped.
wrong_detail: `track.composer NOT LIKE '%Steve Harris%'` is never true when Track.Composer is NULL, so the 978 rows with no Composer are silently left out.

cases.q: What was the total invoiced amount (sum of Invoice.Total) for invoices dated in October 2011 (1 Oct through 31 Oct inclusive)?
cases.mistake: InvoiceDate is stored with a time part ('2011-10-31 00:00:00'), which sorts after '2011-10-31', so the BETWEEN upper bound excludes the invoice on 31 October.
wrong_detail: Invoice.InvoiceDate includes a time of day, so `<= '2011-10-31'` (or BETWEEN … AND '2011-10-31') stops at midnight and drops 1 rows later on 2011-10-31.

cases.q: How many tracks belong to the genre named exactly 'Rock'?
cases.mistake: The wildcard LIKE also matches the separate genre 'Rock And Roll'.
wrong_detail: `Name LIKE '%Rock%'` matches 2 different Name values: ['Rock', 'Rock And Roll']. If you meant one of them, this adds the others too.

cases.q: For every employee who has a manager, list the employee's full name and the full name of the manager they report to (Employee.ReportsTo). Order by employee id.
cases.mistake: The self-join condition is reversed, so it pairs each employee with their direct reports instead of their manager.

cases.q: Which 3 genres have the fewest invoice lines sold? Include genres with zero sales, show the number of invoice lines, and break ties by genre name.
cases.mistake: COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN counts unmatched tracks as rows, so genres with no or few sales get inflated counts (zero-sale genres never show 0).
wrong_detail: COUNT(*) counts 3,759 joined rows, which is more than the rows of any single table (Genre: 25, Track: 3,503, InvoiceLine: 2,240); the joins create combinations (many-to-many).
COUNT(*) counts the row kept for groups with no match, so 'zero' shows as 1.

cases.q: What percentage of all tracks in the catalogue are of media type 'Protected MPEG-4 video file'? Give the percentage rounded to 2 decimal places.
cases.mistake: Integer division truncates the percentage to a whole number before rounding.
wrong_detail: `SUM(CASE WHEN m.name = 'Protected MPEG-4 video file' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100 / COUNT(*)` divides two whole numbers; in sqlite the decimals are thrown away (e.g. 2/3 = 0), so ratios and percentages come out as 0 or rounded down.

cases.q: What was total net revenue for orders placed in 2017 (by OrderDate year), where net revenue = [Order Details].UnitPrice × Quantity × (1 − Discount)? Round to 2 decimals.
cases.mistake: Ignores the Discount column, so it reports gross rather than net revenue.

cases.q: What is the total gross sales amount (price actually charged on the order line × Quantity, no discount) of the product 'Raclette Courdavault' across all orders? Round to 2 decimals.
cases.mistake: Uses the current list price from Products instead of the historical price charged on each order line.

cases.q: What is the total freight cost (Orders.Freight) for each shipper (Shippers.CompanyName)? Order by total freight descending.
cases.mistake: An unnecessary join to order lines repeats each order's freight once per line item, hugely inflating the totals.
wrong_detail: After the joins, each `Orders` row appears 37.42 times on average (609,283 joined rows for 16,282 Orders rows). SUM(o.freight) therefore adds up the same `Orders` rows several times.

cases.q: How many orders were shipped (ShippedDate) in calendar year 2019, per shipper company? Order by shipper name.
cases.mistake: Filters on OrderDate instead of ShippedDate, so it counts orders placed in 2019 rather than shipped in 2019.

cases.q: Which 5 countries have the most orders, where an order's country is the country of the customer who placed it (Customers.Country)? Show country and order count.
cases.mistake: Groups by the order's ShipCountry, which in this data often differs from the customer's own country.

cases.q: What was the average order value for orders placed in 2021, where an order's value is the sum over its lines of UnitPrice × Quantity × (1 − Discount)? Round to 2 decimals.
cases.mistake: Averages individual order lines instead of first totalling each order, giving the average line value rather than the average order value.

cases.q: For each product category, which single product has sold the largest total quantity (sum of [Order Details].Quantity), and what is that quantity? Return category name, product name and quantity, ordered by category name.
cases.mistake: Groups only by category, so the quantity is the whole category's total and the product name is an arbitrary bare column, not the top seller.
wrong_detail: p.productname is selected but not in GROUP BY and not aggregated; SQLite/MySQL return a value from an arbitrary row of each group.

cases.q: How many orders were placed on 16 January 2017 (any time during that day)?
cases.mistake: Exact equality against a date string misses orders whose OrderDate is stored with a time component.
wrong_detail: Orders.OrderDate includes a time of day, so `= '2017-01-16'` only matches rows stored at exactly midnight/without a time (2) and misses 10 of the 12 rows on that day.

cases.q: What is total payment revenue per store, where a payment is credited to the store that owns the rented copy (inventory.store_id via payment.rental_id → rental → inventory)? Order by store_id.
cases.mistake: Attributes payments to the customer's home store (customer.store_id) instead of the store that owns the rented inventory.

cases.q: What is the average film length (minutes) per film category? Each film should count once. Show the top 5 categories by average length, rounded to 2 decimals.
cases.mistake: The film_list view has one row per film-actor pair, so films are weighted by their number of actors (and films without actors are dropped).

cases.q: How many films include 'Deleted Scenes' among their special features?
cases.mistake: special_features is a comma-separated list, so exact equality only finds films whose sole feature is Deleted Scenes.
wrong_detail: film.special_features holds comma-separated lists (e.g. 'Trailers,Commentaries,Behind the Scenes'); `= 'Deleted Scenes'` finds 61 rows where it is the only item, but 503 rows contain it.

cases.q: How many rentals were returned late? A rental is late if the time between rental_date and return_date is strictly greater than the film's rental_duration (in days, measured exactly including hours). Ignore rentals not yet returned.
cases.mistake: Truncating the elapsed days to an integer ignores partial days, so rentals returned a few hours past the due time are not counted as late.

cases.q: Which 5 customers have rented the largest number of distinct films (different titles, not copies)? Show customer_id, name and the count, ties broken by customer_id.
cases.mistake: Counts distinct inventory copies instead of distinct films, so renting two copies of the same title counts twice.

cases.q: What is the average total amount paid per customer (sum each customer's payments, then average across customers)? Round to 2 decimals.
cases.mistake: Averages individual payments instead of per-customer totals.

cases.q: Which 5 actors (individual people, identified by actor_id) appear in the most films? Show actor name and film count, ties broken by actor_id.
cases.mistake: Groups by name instead of actor_id, merging the two different actors both named SUSAN DAVIS into one inflated entry.
wrong_detail: Grouping by first_name, last_name merges different `actor` records that share the same value: e.g. 2 different actor_id values are called 'SUSAN DAVIS'.

cases.q: How many rentals were made from store 1's inventory of films rated 'G' or 'PG'?
cases.mistake: AND binds tighter than OR, so PG rentals from both stores are included.
wrong_detail: `i.store_id = 1 AND f.rating = 'G' OR f.rating = 'PG'` mixes AND and OR without brackets. AND binds first, so this reads as (A AND B) OR C - the OR part ignores the other conditions.
